short_label: Figure 1: Historical compound damage by district
long_caption: Figure 1. District-level compound (wind + surge) expected annual loss under the historical-climate baseline and no-defence profile on the common synthetic catalogue. Pudong, Yangpu, and Minhang are the three largest contributors in absolute loss.

short_label: Figure 2: Compound damage by district — SSP scenarios
long_caption: Figure 2. District-level compound EAL across SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 on the common synthetic catalogue, showing how future scenario forcing raises district losses relative to the historical-climate baseline.
Figure 3. Spatial distribution of TC wind-damage proxy under the historical-climate baseline (no-defence profile; common synthetic catalogue).
Figure 4. District-level TC wind-damage proxy under the historical-climate baseline (no-defence profile).
Figure 5. Surge event occurrence frequency (events with inundation > 0.05 m) under the historical-climate baseline (no-defence profile).
Figure 6. District-level storm-surge damage proxy under the historical-climate baseline (no-defence profile).

Figure 7. Shanghai Climate Risk Index (CRI): historical series 1993–2023 and SDE Monte Carlo forward projections to 2050 under three scenarios. Shaded bands show the 10th–90th percentile ensemble range; solid lines indicate the representative (characteristic) path.

Figure 8. Shanghai Housing Stress Index (HSI), 2011–2025. The HSI rises from 100 to approximately 231 over the observation period and reaches its historical maximum in February 2023, when elevated realised volatility and climate-tail-risk conditions coincide.
Figure 9. Decomposition of the HSI into its three sub-indicators: price gap (HP deviation), realised volatility, and climate CVaR. Each contributes one-third to the composite.
Figure 10. Shanghai residential housing price (CNY/m²) with Hodrick–Prescott trend (, Ravn–Uhlig monthly convention). Persistent positive gaps indicate overvaluation risk.

Figure 11. Historical CRI and HSI overlay (2011-12 to 2023-12), demonstrating co-movement that motivates the compound index construction. The reported  is the calibrated dependence target used in trajectory-level pairing; realised paired-path rank correlation is checked diagnostically and is expected to be close to, rather than exactly equal to, that target.
Figure 12. Composite Climate-Housing Index (CCHI): historical series and Monte Carlo projections. The geometric-mean construction ensures balanced sensitivity to both risk channels.

short_label: Figure 13: Triple comparison — CRI, HSI, CCHI
long_caption: Figure 13. Joint time series of CRI, HSI, and CCHI, showing co-evolution and the moderating effect of geometric-mean aggregation.
Figure 14. CCHI decomposition into CRI and HSI component contributions across scenarios.

short_label: Figure 16: Historical TC tracks over Shanghai
long_caption: Figure 16. Historical TC tracks crossing the Shanghai study domain, colour-coded by maximum sustained wind speed (m/s).

short_label: Figure 17: Storm surge inundation depth — historical
long_caption: Figure 17. Spatial distribution of maximum storm-surge inundation depth (m) across Shanghai under the historical-climate baseline and no-defence profile on the common synthetic catalogue. Inland positive depths should be interpreted as the theoretical inundation reach of the zero-crest reference state used for defence-benefit estimation, rather than as a present-day defended flood map. Hexagonal binning at 0.01° resolution.
Figure 18. Spatial distribution of storm-surge damage proxy (CNY) under the historical-climate baseline and no-defence profile, showing concentration in low-lying coastal and riverine districts.

Figure 19. TC wind impact functions (Emanuel sigmoid) for the six building categories, showing mean damage ratio (MDR) as a function of wind speed. Category A_old (pre-1990 low-rise) is most vulnerable; Category D (commercial) is most resistant.
Figure 20. Storm-surge depth–damage functions for the four building surge classes, calibrated from HAZUS-MH. Low-rise structures sustain the highest MDR at equivalent inundation depths.

short_label: Figure 21: Study area overview showing Shanghai’s 16 districts, building exposure distribution, and key geographic features
long_caption: Figure 21. Study area overview: Shanghai Municipality with building-level exposure distribution by value class, Huangpu River corridor, and East China Sea coastline. Building data derived from municipal GIS footprint shapefiles with three-tier market valuation.
Figure 22. Annual count of tropical cyclone events affecting the Shanghai region (within 3.0° radius), based on the 107-event catalogue for 1945–2025. Source: IBTrACS WP v04r01.
Figure 23. Monthly distribution of the 107 TC events affecting Shanghai. Activity is concentrated in July–September and peaks in August, consistent with western North Pacific seasonality.

Figure 24. Defence-sensitivity evidence from the active model outputs. Left: city-wide EAL decomposition by scenario and defence profile, showing that the wind component is unchanged across profiles while the surge component falls sharply under the current 6 m defence standard. Right: district-level historical EAL reduction rates, showing that mitigation is spatially heterogeneous and strongest in surge-dominated districts.
Figure 25. Synthetic TC tracks derived from 10 perturbations per historical track, showing the expanded spatial sampling used in the scenario runs.

short_label: Figure 26: TC damage hexbin — SSP scenarios
long_caption: Figure 26. TC wind-damage fields for SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 based on the synthetic catalogue.

short_label: Figure 27: Surge depth hexbin — SSP scenarios
long_caption: Figure 27. Storm-surge inundation fields for SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 based on the synthetic catalogue and the same no-defence reference profile. As in Figure 17, inland positive depths denote the modelled reach of the zero-crest counterfactual used for comparative defence accounting, not present-day defended inundation conditions.
Figure 28. Full historical TC track inventory for the Shanghai region.
Figure 29. Spatial distribution of TC wind vulnerability (effective ) across the building stock.
Figure 30. Spatial distribution of storm-surge depth–damage vulnerability by building class.
Figure 31. Multi-decadal evolution of built-up area / impervious surface ratio in Shanghai, documenting the urbanisation trajectory that drives increasing runoff amplification.
Figure 32. Historical housing price evolution across Shanghai districts.
Figure 33. Shanghai population trends from LandScan data, 2000–2024.
Figure 34. Spatial distribution of building categories across Shanghai’s districts. Pre-1990 low-rise structures (A_old) concentrate in central riverine districts.

Figure 35. Vulnerability function overview with sensitivity ranges. (a) TC wind impact functions for all six building categories at baseline  scale. (b) Storm-surge depth–damage functions for all four building classes; solid lines show the baseline calibration (×0.176) and shaded bands span the tested range [0.10, 0.30].

Figure 36. TC wind vulnerability sensitivity to  base scale. Panels show the Emanuel sigmoid for (a) A_old and (b) C under five scale values [0.95, 0.975, 1.0, 1.025, 1.05]. The solid yellow line marks the baseline; dashed lines show perturbations. The vertical grey line indicates the baseline damage onset threshold (25.7 m/s).

Figure 37. TC wind vulnerability sensitivity to the damage onset threshold . Panels show the Emanuel sigmoid for (a) A_old and (b) C under five threshold values [23.0, 24.5, 25.7, 27.0, 28.5] m/s. The effect is concentrated in the low-wind regime and diminishes at higher speeds.

Figure 38. Storm-surge depth–damage sensitivity to the MDR calibration scale. Each panel shows one building class (a: low-rise, b: mid-rise, c: high-rise, d: commercial) under five calibration scale values [0.10, 0.14, 0.176, 0.22, 0.30]. The solid yellow line marks the baseline; dashed lines show perturbations.
